title: Inside a decoder: from text to the next token
summary: Trace every tensor through a decoder transformer, calculate attention by hand, and defend the architectural choices behind autoregressive language models.
learningObjectives: Trace token IDs, hidden states, attention heads, and vocabulary logits with explicit shapes.
Calculate a masked attention row and a next-token distribution.
Explain position, normalization, residual paths, and gated MLPs without treating them as interchangeable.
Distinguish parallel teacher-forced training from sequential generation and reusable inference state.

sections.title: 1. The model's contract is conditional prediction
paragraphs: Let's start with what the model actually does. A decoder language model (the kind of transformer behind LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude) assigns a distribution to the next token given a prefix. In plain terms, it looks at the text so far and gives every possible next token a probability, a bit like a very well-read autocomplete. A token is a small chunk of text, often a word or a piece of one, and before the model sees anything each token is swapped for an integer called a token ID. We'll look at how that text-to-ID step works in section 2. A chat interface supplies that prefix by serializing messages, role delimiters (special markers for who is speaking), and any tool results into a model-specific template. The transformer does not receive an intrinsic JavaScript conversation object. Its input is a sequence of IDs, plus position and masking information, both of which we'll cover later in this article. Getting this boundary right helps you avoid a common interview mistake: attributing application behavior such as authorization or durable memory to the neural network itself. The formula below writes the same idea down: the probability of a whole sequence is a chain of these next-token predictions multiplied together.

With that contract in place, let's look at the overall shape of the model. It helps to name a few sizes first. Let B be batch size (how many sequences run together), T sequence length (tokens per sequence), d hidden width (how many numbers represent each token), and V vocabulary size (how many distinct tokens the tokenizer knows). An input has shape B × T; embedding lookup, which swaps each ID for a learned vector of d numbers, produces B × T × d; a stack of L decoder blocks preserves that shape. A final vocabulary projection produces B × T × V logits, which are raw scores, one per vocabulary entry, that section 6 turns into probabilities. At inference, the last relevant position predicts the next token. A bit of history explains the name: the original transformer was built for translation and had an encoder that read the source sentence plus a decoder that consulted it through cross-attention. A decoder-only stack normally omits that cross-attention to a separate encoder. [The original architecture](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7) is therefore a foundation, not a literal specification of every chat model. The walkthrough below follows three token rows through this pipeline with tiny made-up numbers. Don't worry yet about what happens inside the block (attention, the MLP, normalization, RoPE); sections 3 through 5 unpack each piece, and the figure at the end of this section recaps the whole shape contract.

sections.title: 2. Tokenization is an architectural interface
paragraphs: Now let's back up to the very first step: turning text into the token IDs we saw in section 1. A token is not necessarily a word. Subword tokenizers represent common strings compactly while decomposing less common strings into smaller units, so a frequent word might be one token while a rare one gets split into a few pieces. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) learns merge rules by starting from small units and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new vocabulary entry; the trained tokenizer applies those rules deterministically under its configuration. Byte-level representations (working on raw bytes rather than characters) and byte fallback (dropping to individual bytes when nothing in the vocabulary matches) are related ways to improve coverage, but neither should be assumed for an arbitrary vocabulary. The [subword paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909) motivates decomposing rare words; the [Tokenizers components documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers/main/en/components) distinguishes normalization, pre-tokenization, the tokenization model, and post-processing (the figure at the end of this section lays out those stages). The walkthrough below uses a tiny invented vocabulary to show a string becoming pieces, then IDs.

This interface has practical consequences. A change in whitespace, Unicode normalization, or a role delimiter can change the token sequence. Code, identifiers, and different languages can require very different token counts for visually similar amounts of text. A context limit applies to tokens, so character-count budgeting is only an estimate. It also means the tokenizer and chat template are effectively part of the model. A checkpoint learned its weights from the exact ID sequences its own tokenizer and template produced, so pairing it with a different tokenizer, or even a slightly different template, hands it sequences unlike anything it saw in training, and output quality can drop even though not a single weight has changed.

Once we have IDs, the model needs vectors it can do math on, and that's the job of the embedding table. The embedding table E has V rows and d columns. You can think of it as a big lookup sheet: the ID is the row number, and that row holds the token's starting vector. Token ID 17 selects row 17; it is not the scalar number 17 multiplied by a vector. For a hypothetical V=50,000 and d=4,096, the table contains 204,800,000 parameters, or 409,600,000 bytes in two-byte storage, approximately 390.6 MiB. That excludes gradients, optimizer state, and runtime buffers. There is a second table of the same size at the other end of the model. The vocabulary projection from section 1 scores every possible next token by taking the final hidden vector and computing its dot product with one learned d-number vector per vocabulary entry; those V dot products are the logits. That V × d matrix is often called the output embedding, because it also holds one vector per token. The two tables answer different questions: the input embedding asks 'what vector should represent this token going in?', while the output embedding asks 'what final hidden state should make this token likely to come next?'. A model can learn the two separately, or it can tie them, meaning the output projection simply reuses E, so one table serves as the lookup at the start and the scoring matrix at the end. Tying saves a whole second allocation (another ~390.6 MiB in this example) and is common in smaller models, where the vocabulary tables are a large share of all parameters. Keeping them untied costs that memory but lets each table specialize for its own job. Which choice a model uses is fixed by its architecture, not something you toggle later. The walkthrough below selects a row, draws it as an arrow, and stacks a short sequence into the position-by-feature grid the rest of the model works on.

sections.title: 3. Attention routes information between positions
paragraphs: At this point each token is a row of numbers, but each row only knows about its own token. Attention is the step that lets positions share information. For one attention head, learned projections map hidden states (the per-token vectors flowing through the model, starting from the embeddings) to queries Q, keys K, and values Vh. We write Vh so it doesn't clash with the vocabulary size V. A loose analogy is a search: each position writes a query describing what it's looking for, every position advertises a key describing what it has, and the value is the content handed over when the match is good. Unlike a real dictionary lookup, the match is soft, so every permitted position can contribute a little. Queries and keys determine compatibility; values supply the vectors that are mixed. With head dimension dₕ, Q and K have shape T × dₕ for one sequence. Their product creates T × T scores. Softmax (exponentiate each score, then divide by the total so the row becomes positive weights summing to one) acts across permitted source positions separately for each query. In causal attention, position i can use positions j≤i, so no token peeks at tokens after it; later positions receive a negative-infinity mask before softmax, which turns into a weight of exactly zero. See [scaled dot-product attention](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7). The two walkthroughs below first build Q, K, and V from a single hidden row, then turn query/key dot products into a masked score grid.

Now let's calculate one row explicitly. Here the scores have already been divided by √dₕ (the scaling we'll justify in a moment). Suppose a query has three permitted scaled scores [2,1,0], and the three value vectors are [1,0], [0,2], and [2,2]. Subtracting the maximum gives exponentials [1,0.3679,0.1353]; dividing by their sum gives weights approximately [0.6652,0.2447,0.0900]. The output is therefore [0.8453,0.6695]. A fourth, future position gets zero probability regardless of its unmasked score. This is a weighted mixture of learned vectors, not a lookup that copies the most likely source token. The walkthrough below animates this exact calculation, and the bar chart at the end of this section shows the same weights.

So far we've looked at a single head. Real models run several heads side by side, a bit like a few reviewers reading the same document, each paying attention to different things. Multiple heads learn different projections and mix their outputs through an output projection. With d=4,096 and 32 equal query heads, each head has width 128, and concatenating the 32 head outputs brings the width back to 4,096. The walkthrough below splits a toy four-wide row into two heads, mixes each independently, and joins them back together.

Head width also explains the √dₕ in the formula below. Under the simplifying assumption that independent query/key components have zero mean and unit variance, an unscaled dot product has variance 128. Dividing by √128 restores variance near one, helping avoid immediate softmax saturation (where one score is so large that softmax puts nearly all the weight on it and gradients almost vanish). Real trained activations need not satisfy those assumptions exactly; the derivation explains the scale factor rather than proving every model is normalized.
sections.formula: Attention(Q,K,Vh) = softmax(QKᵀ / √dₕ + M)Vh; Mᵢⱼ = 0 if j≤i, otherwise −∞

sections.title: 4. Position supplies order, not unlimited context
paragraphs: You might have noticed that nothing in the attention math so far knows about word order. A content-only attention score cannot directly distinguish otherwise identical tokens at different locations. Position representations supply that missing information. Learned absolute embeddings add a position-dependent vector; sinusoidal embeddings add deterministic frequencies (fixed sine and cosine waves). Rotary position embedding (RoPE) instead rotates pairs of query and key coordinates as a function of position. The resulting dot product incorporates relative displacement. A rough analogy is a pair of clock hands: each token's query or key gets turned by an amount based on its position, and comparing two hands only depends on the angle between them, so what matters is how far apart two tokens are rather than where they sit. [RoFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864) derives this property; it does not establish that arbitrary context lengths will work equally well. The walkthrough below shows both styles: adding a position vector to the input, then rotating query/key pairs.

To see why rotation encodes relative position, consider a two-dimensional pair initially [1,0]. Rotating it by 0 radians gives [1,0], and by π/2 gives [0,1]. Their dot product changes from one for matching angles to zero at that offset. Real RoPE applies multiple frequencies across coordinate pairs. This small construction explains the mechanism without implying tokens literally occupy a physical circle. A longer configured context changes the positions and dependencies encountered by the model; quality still depends on training, scaling choices, and evaluation. Test retrieval at different depths and distractor densities (for example, hiding a fact at various points in a long prompt full of irrelevant text) before promising long-context reliability. The figure at the end of this section compares all three approaches side by side.

sections.title: 5. Residuals, normalization, and MLPs do different jobs
paragraphs: With attention and position covered, let's open up the rest of the decoder block. Each block has two sublayers: attention, and an MLP (a small feed-forward network applied to each token separately, covered at the end of this section). In a typical pre-normalized block, meaning normalization happens before each sublayer rather than after, attention reads a normalized residual stream and adds an update back to the original stream. The MLP does the same in a second sublayer. One way to picture the residual stream is a shared notebook passed from layer to layer: each sublayer reads a tidied-up copy and writes a note in the margin, rather than rewriting the whole page. The residual path gives features and gradients a route that does not require every sublayer to reconstruct the entire representation. Normalization controls activation scale; it does not store a conversation or normalize over the vocabulary. The [LLaMA paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.13971v1) describes a concrete decoder using pre-normalization, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and rotary embeddings (RMSNorm and SwiGLU are explained below). The walkthrough below follows one token's numbers through both residual additions, and the figure at the end of this section lays out the full block.

Next up is normalization. LayerNorm centers a token's feature vector and scales by its standard deviation, with learned affine parameters. RMSNorm rescales using root mean square without subtracting the feature mean. For x=[3,4], ignoring epsilon and using unit gain, RMS=√12.5≈3.5355, so RMSNorm returns approximately [0.8485,1.1314]. LayerNorm on the same vector, under the same simplifying assumptions, returns [-1,1]. This calculated difference shows why replacing one with the other changes the function. [RMSNorm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467) motivates dropping the centering step. The walkthrough below computes both on this same vector.

Finally, the MLP. Attention mixes positions; a standard dense MLP transforms features independently at each position using shared weights. A SwiGLU MLP multiplies a SiLU-activated projection by a second projection, then projects back to d. SiLU is a smooth activation, z times sigmoid(z), that behaves a lot like ReLU but without the sharp corner. You can think of the gate as a row of dimmer switches, one per feature, rather than on/off switches. The gate is continuous, not a discrete expert router (the kind used in mixture-of-experts models, covered in the Mixture of Experts and Parallelism article). Its three matrices require approximately 3dm parameters when the intermediate width is m, compared with 2dm for a two-matrix MLP of that same width. Match parameter budgets before attributing an improvement entirely to activation choice. [GLU variants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202) provide the experimental motivation for gated feed-forward layers. The walkthrough below expands one token into gate and value branches, multiplies them, and projects back to the original width.
sections.formula: u = x + Attention(Norm(x)); y = u + MLP(Norm(u)); SwiGLU(x) = [SiLU(xWg) ⊙ (xWu)]Wd

sections.title: 6. Logits become decisions through a decoding policy
paragraphs: We've now followed a token all the way through the stack, so the last step is turning the final hidden state into an actual choice. The final hidden state is projected to V logits, real-valued scores with no requirement to sum to one. Softmax (the same operation attention used, now applied across the vocabulary instead of across positions) converts these to probabilities. Temperature τ is a knob that divides the logits before softmax: lower values sharpen the distribution, higher values flatten it. For logits [2,1,0] and temperature τ=1, probabilities are [0.6652,0.2447,0.0900]. At τ=0.5, the scaled logits [4,2,0] produce approximately [0.8668,0.1173,0.0159]. Temperature changes concentration without changing rank for positive τ. It does not add knowledge, correct a false premise, or calibrate factual confidence. The walkthrough below projects a hidden row to three toy logits, applies softmax at both temperatures, and previews the filtering step we'll discuss next.

Once you have probabilities, you still need a rule for picking a token, which is called the decoding policy. Greedy decoding selects the highest-scoring next token. Sampling draws from a distribution, often after top-k or nucleus filtering. Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens; nucleus (top-p) filtering keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to a threshold. With the first distribution above, nucleus threshold 0.9 retains the first two tokens because their cumulative mass is approximately 0.9099, then renormalizes them. Greedy decisions need not maximize the probability of the entire completed sequence. Stop tokens, maximum output length, repetition controls, and structured-output constraints are additional policy choices. The [generation guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/generation_strategies) separates these methods; save their configuration with an experiment so comparisons are reproducible. The formula below shows temperature-scaled softmax, and the figure at the end of this section compares temperature 1, temperature 0.5, and greedy selection on the same logits.
sections.formula: pᵢ = exp((zᵢ − max(z))/τ) / Σⱼ exp((zⱼ − max(z))/τ), for τ>0

sections.title: 7. Parallel training and sequential inference share one model
paragraphs: To wrap up, let's connect training and generation, since the same model runs in two quite different modes. Training usually uses teacher forcing, which means feeding the model the true previous tokens rather than its own guesses. During teacher-forced training, the full observed sequence is available. Inputs [A,B,C] can predict targets [B,C,D] in one masked forward pass; each position remains forbidden from seeing its future target. Average negative log probability of the targets gives cross-entropy, the standard training loss (lower is better). If target probabilities are 0.5, 0.25, and 0.125, mean loss is about 1.3863 nats (natural-log units) and perplexity is exp(loss)=4. Perplexity is roughly how many tokens the model is choosing between on average, so 4 means it behaves as if it were picking among about four equally likely options. These are calculated values for an invented sequence. A suspiciously low loss can signal a missing causal mask or incorrectly shifted labels rather than an excellent model.

Generation works differently, because it cannot know the next sampled ID in advance. It processes the prefix, chooses a token, appends it, and repeats. Processing the known prompt is often called prefill, and the token-by-token loop after it is called decode. In causal inference, prior positions do not change when later tokens are appended, so each layer can reuse their projected keys and values. Storing them for reuse is what's called a KV cache. It's a bit like keeping notes on the pages you've already read, instead of rereading the whole book every time you turn a page. The new query still attends over those cached positions. [Hugging Face's cache explanation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/cache_explanation) describes this reuse, and the Serving LLMs: KV Cache as a Memory and Latency Budget article goes much deeper. A KV cache is model execution state tied to an exact prefix and model configuration; it is not a durable conversation database or a cache of finished answers. The walkthrough below shows the shifted training targets first, then a cache that grows by one row per generated token.

How big does that cache get? Here Hkv is the number of key/value heads; in ordinary multi-head attention it equals the number of query heads, while variants that share KV heads are covered in the Efficient Attention: Heads, Memory Traffic, and Context article. The leading 2 counts keys and values separately. For ordinary multi-head attention, a cache estimate is 2 × L × B × T × Hkv × dₕ × bytes_per_element. With 32 layers, one sequence, 4,096 cached tokens, 32 KV heads, head width 128, and two-byte elements, that is 2,147,483,648 bytes, or 2 GiB, excluding allocator overhead. This original sizing example makes the architectural stakes tangible: reducing KV heads changes memory, whereas merely lowering sampling temperature does not. Use exact checkpoint dimensions when planning capacity. The figure at the end of this section summarizes where parallelism is available across training, prefill, and decode.

interview.question: A teammate says doubling the context window is harmless because the model has unchanged parameter count, and a KV cache makes generation constant-time. How do you respond?
interview.answer: Separate weights from runtime state. For dense causal attention, doubling prefix length roughly quadruples the pairwise attention work during prefill, while projection and MLP work grow linearly in token count. The KV cache grows linearly with cached tokens. Each ordinary decode query must still read and attend across its relevant cached prefix, so cache reuse removes recomputation of prior keys and values without making context-independent latency. Kernel behavior, memory bandwidth, batching, and attention variants affect observed scaling. I would calculate KV bytes using the checkpoint's KV head count, measure time to first token and per-token latency at representative lengths, and evaluate answer quality at long positions rather than assuming a configured limit guarantees useful recall.
followUps: What changes if the model uses grouped-query attention?
How would a broken padding mask differ from a broken causal mask?
Which cached entries remain valid when a user edits an earlier message?

pitfalls: Treating token IDs as ordered numeric features instead of lookup indices.
Confusing attention weights over positions with vocabulary probabilities over next tokens.
Applying causal masking after softmax without correct renormalization.
Assuming every decoder reproduces the original encoder-decoder paper exactly.
Using low temperature as a substitute for factual validation.
Reusing a KV cache after changing its prefix, model, or position interpretation.
checklist: Write B, T, d, V, head count, and head width before reasoning about tensors.
Inspect tokenizer version, special tokens, and the complete chat template.
Check shifted targets, causal masking, padding behavior, and loss masking separately.
State normalization placement and the actual MLP variant.
Calculate weight memory and KV memory as separate allocations.
Record decoding settings and evaluate quality alongside latency.

flashcards.front: What does a decoder language model directly predict?
flashcards.back: A next-token distribution conditioned on a token prefix. Conversation roles and tools enter through serialization; the model does not intrinsically manage application state.

flashcards.front: What are the input, hidden-state, and logit shapes?
flashcards.back: B × T IDs become B × T × d hidden states and B × T × V logits. The last valid position supplies next-token logits during generation.

flashcards.front: Why can equal-length strings consume different context budgets?
flashcards.back: A tokenizer segments using its learned vocabulary and preprocessing. Characters, words, and tokens are different units, especially across languages and code.

flashcards.front: How much storage does a 50,000 × 4,096 embedding table require at two bytes per parameter?
flashcards.back: 204.8 million parameters occupy 409.6 million bytes, about 390.6 MiB, excluding gradients and other state. Tying the output projection can avoid a second matrix.

flashcards.front: Why are keys and values separate?
flashcards.back: Keys participate in compatibility scores with queries; values are the information vectors mixed using those scores. Separate projections allow routing and payload to differ.
Under independent unit-variance components, dot-product variance grows as dₕ. Scaling controls that growth and reduces softmax saturation; the assumptions are an explanatory approximation.

flashcards.front: Where does the causal mask enter?
flashcards.back: Before softmax, forbidden source scores become negative infinity so they receive zero probability. This prevents future-target leakage while training many positions together.

flashcards.front: What does RoPE rotate, and what does it not guarantee?
flashcards.back: It rotates query/key coordinate pairs by position-dependent angles, producing relative-position effects in their dot products. It does not guarantee useful behavior at arbitrary context lengths.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes residual connections from normalization?
flashcards.back: Residual additions preserve a direct stream and gradient route while sublayers add updates. Normalization controls feature scale; the two solve different problems.

flashcards.front: How does RMSNorm differ from LayerNorm?
flashcards.back: RMSNorm rescales using root mean square without subtracting the feature mean. LayerNorm centers and rescales, so swapping them changes the network function.

flashcards.front: Does a standard transformer MLP mix token positions?
flashcards.back: No. It applies shared feature transformations independently at each position. Attention supplies cross-position mixing; gated MLPs modulate features with continuous products.

flashcards.front: What does lowering positive temperature change?
flashcards.back: It sharpens the next-token probability distribution without changing logit ordering. This changes sampling behavior, not the model's knowledge or factual calibration.

flashcards.front: Why can training predict multiple positions at once but ordinary generation cannot?
flashcards.back: Teacher forcing supplies the observed prefix at every training position, with causal masking. At inference, each chosen next token is needed before the following conditional distribution can be evaluated.

flashcards.front: What does a KV cache save, and what work remains?
flashcards.back: It stores prior projected keys and values per layer. New tokens avoid recomputing that state but must still compute their own states and attend over applicable cached positions.
